historical_record.description: Works Progress Administration crews deposited 20,000 cubic yards of fill here and built the stone seawall, the bathhouse, the beach, two boathouses and retaining walls, paving 101,000 square feet of concrete promenade.

The Aquatic Park Bathhouse holds one of the city's densest concentrations of Federal Art Project work: Hilaire Hiler's Prismatarium and his Lost Continents of Atlantis and Mu, Sargent Johnson's incised slate marquee, ceramic lintel and tile sea forms, Richard Ayer's Nautical Abstractions and Tugboats, Charles Nunemaker's Sepia Seascape and Beniamino Bufano's granite Frog and Seal of 1942.
Recommended for city landmark designation in 2023, on historical, aesthetic and artistic grounds.

Sargent Johnson's slate frieze is here, along with the tile mosaic on the second-storey veranda that he left unfinished in 1939 when he walked away from the project. The building is part of the Aquatic Park National Historic Landmark District.

The Aquatic Park Bathhouse, designed by William Mooser II and William Mooser III as a Works Progress Administration project, was completed after work began in 1936; Hilaire Hiler designed the lobby and Prismatarium murals.
The city cancelled the concessioners' lease on the bathhouse after a WPA investigation into the unfinished project, which had driven several artists, Sargent Johnson among them, to walk off the job.
The Army used the bathhouse as a headquarters until January 1946, first for the 216th Coast Artillery Regiment and then for the whole Fourth Anti-Aircraft Command.
The Senior Center opened in the Blue Room at the east end of the second floor.
The San Francisco Maritime Museum opened in the lobby, the Prismatarium and the upper floors.
The bathhouse and the Maritime Museum came under the National Park Service, in the new maritime unit of the Golden Gate National Recreation Area.

The museum's exhibits were removed for a project repairing the roofs and replacing the windows; taking out the 1970s exhibit walls on the third floor exposed what remained of the original artwork. The lobby murals were conserved in 2009-2011, the Prismatarium in 2012-2013, and the Blue Room restored in 2014.

At the dedication of Aquatic Park on Sunday, January 22, 1939, the State Administrator of the Works Progress Administration turned the bathhouse building and the other improvements built by WPA labor over to the Mayor, who transferred them to the Board of Park Commissioners.
